1.
INTRODUCTION
PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THE EVALUATION
The purpose of this ex-post evaluation is to assess the outputs and outcomes achieved by the
Consumer Programme 2014-20201 (hereinafter ‘Programme’), and the progress made towards
the set objectives and its longer impact. It focuses on the five evaluation criteria: effectiveness,
efficiency, relevance, coherence, and the EU added value of the actions funded. Where
applicable, further evaluation criteria were applied: utility, complementarity, equity,
coordination, sustainability, and acceptability.
It covers the period between 2014 and 2020, while building up on the findings, conclusions,
and recommendations of the mid-term evaluation2. The mid-term evaluation covered the period
between 2014 and 2017. It considers the implementation of the Programme in all EU countries,
as well as in Norway and Iceland3. The evaluation exercise provides the necessary space for
reflection on whether the Programme had been flexible to respond to the needs of its
stakeholders, i.e. consumer organisations, Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC)
authorities, European Consumers Centres (ECC) who are its direct beneficiaries, and
consumers who benefit from a better implemented and enforced consumer law. It identifies the
main problems in its implementation and lessons learned.
This retrospective evaluation meets the legal obligation set out in Article 34 of the Financial
Regulation (EU) No 2018/10464. The Financial Regulation requires an evaluation of all
programmes and activities that entail significant overall spending. While it does not define the
level of the ‘significant spending’, the Better Regulation guidelines set an indicative threshold
at least at EUR 5 million. The Programme was a continuation of the Consumer Programme
2007-2013. It is closed now, while most of its activities continue to be funded under the Single
Market Programme 2021-2027, albeit with some necessary adaptations5. To the extent possible
the evaluation findings will feed into the design of the Multi-annual Financial Framework
2028-2034.
The evaluation applied a mixed-method approach, including desk reviews of literature,
programme documentation, and a sample of grants and procurement files. Stakeholder input
was gathered via a call for evidence, an online survey of beneficiaries (n = 57), targeted

The evaluation faced several methodological and data-related challenges, which were mitigated
to the extent possible through triangulation and additional data collection. These limitations
include:
•
Data governance issues: Administrative changes during the Programme period led to
incomplete or inconsistent programme management data, particularly in project
tracking.
•
Data accessibility and quality concerns: Funding and performance data, especially for
procurement contracts, were manually recorded, often lacking standardisation, which
affected reliability and comparability across actions.
•
Stakeholder participation deficits: The overall response rate to the consultation tools
was low. The online survey had only 57 responses, mainly from beneficiaries, which
limits the generalisability of the findings.
•
Methodological limitations in indicator design: The Programme relied heavily on
output-based indicators as set in Annex II of the Regulation. These were not
systematically complemented by outcome or impact indicators, limiting the capacity to
assess behavioural or systemic effects.
Despite this multi-source approach, the evaluation encountered major data limitations.
Baselines for several outcome and impact-level indicators were missing or poorly defined at
the outset of the Programme. For example, there was no shared baseline for consumer detriment
beyond the one-off Consumer Detriment Study, no standardised data on whether businesses
changed their compliance behaviour because of Programme-funded actions. While awareness
and reach of campaigns were tracked, behavioural follow-up was rare, and longitudinal data to
assess sustained effects were absent. Business-side data were also lacking, except for proxy
indicators from CPC sweeps or RAPEX reactions. Inconsistencies in Member State reporting,
especially within the CPC system, further limited the ability to assess cross-country effects.
The ODR platform itself lacked integrated monitoring of user satisfaction, case quality, or
reasons for complaint attrition, making it difficult to assess outcome quality.

approach to assess causal links. Triangulation of qualitative and quantitative data supported the

2.
WHAT WAS THE EXPECTED OUTCOME OF THE INTERVENTION?
2.1 Policy context
Article 169 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union requires the EU to
contribute to protecting the health, safety, and economic interests of consumers through actions
in the field of consumer protection and also to take consumer protection requirements into
account in defining and implementing other Union policies and activities. Besides the
possibility to adopt legislative proposals in the context of completion of the internal market,
the EU may adopt measures to support, supplement and monitor the policy pursued at national
level to promote consumers’ rights to information, education and to organise themselves. The
Commission outlined its strategic vision for EU consumer policy in the European Consumer
Agenda8. To support the European Consumer Agenda and to cope with the challenges outlined
in it, the Commission adopted a multi-annual Consumer Programme for the years 2014-2020.
The Programme contained targeted policies that contributed to the 2030 Agenda for
Sustainable Development9, concretely to its Goal 12 on Sustainable Consumption and
Production and Goal 3 on Ensuring Healthy Lives.
2.2 Description of the intervention and its objectives
Key challenges that the Programme was meant to address were identified in its 2011 impact
assessment10:
1. Product safety: Uneven enforcement across Member States and the lack of a pan-European
framework compromised the safety of the Single Market. Global supply chains increased risks,
while the absence of EU-level coordination reduced the value of co-financing.
2. Consumer information and education: Inadequate data on consumer behaviour, weak
capacity of consumer organisations (especially in newer Member States), and lack of clear,
comparable information hindered consumer decision-making, particularly in cross-border
contexts. EU tools were not adapted to digital developments.
3. Consumer rights and redress: Consumer protection remained weak in cross-border
situations, with low confidence in online shopping and limited awareness of redress
mechanisms. There was also a need to better integrate consumer interests into EU policies,
including digitalisation, sustainability, and social inclusion.
4. Enforcement: the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network was underutilised, with
untapped potential for coordination. Moreover, the European Consumer Centres Network
(ECC-Net) lacked visibility, and needed strengthening to more effectively support cross-border
complain resolution.
The Programme’s intervention logic (see Figure 1) illustrates how its objectives, resources,
and outputs are expected to generate results, based on key assumptions for success. It responds
to a context of weak market monitoring, under-resourced consumer organisations, and limited

To address these challenges, the Programme aimed to ensure a high level of consumer
protection, empower consumers, and place them at the centre of the internal market, in line
with the Europe 2020 strategy (Article 2 of the Programme Regulation). It sought to protect
consumers’ health, safety, and economic interests, promote their rights to information and
education, and support the integration of consumer interests into other policy areas. The
Programme complemented and supported Member State policies and was structured around
four specific objectives and 11 action types (Article 4 and Annex I), further detailed in 40
activities (see Table 1). Funded actions addressed digitalisation, information complexity,
sustainability, and diverse consumer vulnerabilities.

logic linked inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and long-term impacts, while also making
key assumptions about how and why the intervention would work. The evaluation used this
logic to systematically test whether causal links materialised and whether these assumptions
held in practice.
The intervention logic followed a theory-of-change structure:
→ If the Programme funded cross-border cooperation and enforcement tools (e.g. CPC,
ECC-Net),
→ Then Member States would better enforce consumer protection rules,
→ Which leads to greater consumer confidence and protection in the Single Market.
Objective I: Funding for coordinated actions on product safety → better market surveillance
→ fewer unsafe products.
Each of the Programme’s specific objectives followed a distinct causal pathway. Under
Objective I, the Programme funded activities such as scientific risk assessments, data-sharing
mechanisms, and market surveillance coordination, particularly through the Safety
Gate/RAPEX system. The underlying assumption was that more timely and accurate
information would enable national authorities to respond more effectively to unsafe products,
while at the same time providing for cost saving, as testing did not have to be repeated across
Member States. This was explored in the evaluation using Safety Gate/RAPEX data, which
indicated that the proportion of reactions to alerts increased substantially, from 39% at baseline
to over 70% by the end of the Programme. The Coordinated Actions for the Safety of Products
(CASP) provided complementary evidence through coordinated testing, joint risk assessments,
and market surveillance campaigns. Results of all activites can be found in Safety Gate/RAPEX
and ICSMS, but most importantly trust and methods of cooperation between MSAs was
fostered, and common risk assessment methodologies were developed. Complex or novel
products that provided a challenge to MSAs were also addressed in CASP. Despite those
actions being a step towards improved product safety across the EU, enforcement responses
varied considerably across Member States, reflecting differences in administrative capacity and
prioritisation. The available evidence suggests that the causal link between alerts and consumer
protection was stronger where authorities acted promptly, and weaker in Member States with
limited resources or follow-up mechanisms.
Objective II: Consumer education tools → increased knowledge of rights → more confident
and empowered consumers.
Objective II addressed consumer awareness, education, and support for civil society actors such
as consumer organisations. Activities included Europe-wide awareness campaigns, market
studies, and capacity-building support to national and EU-level organisations. The underlying
assumption was that better-informed consumers would make more confident and rational
decisions, thereby reducing the incidence of detriment and improving trust in the market. The
evaluation tested this logic through Consumer Conditions Scoreboard data and campaign
metrics. Within this logic, campaigns like #YourEUright aimed to reach large audiences across
the EU to increase knowledge of rights, while capacity-building support to organisations such
as BEUC sought to strengthen their ability to advocate for consumers and engage in
3
policymaking at both EU and national levels. The causal pathway therefore linked large-scale
information provision and enhanced organisational capacity to intermediate outcomes such as
higher consumer awareness, stronger representation, and ultimately more informed consumer
choices and improved market trust.
Objective III: Development and promotion of ADR/ODR mechanisms → better access to
redress → reduced need for court procedures.
Under Objective III, the Programme aimed to improve access to redress through actions such
as the development of the Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) platform and support for national
Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) schemes. The assumption was that increasing access to
easy, low-cost dispute mechanisms would reduce unresolved complaints and increase
consumer satisfaction. This assumption was tested using ODR usage statistics and ADR uptake
data. Within this logic, the ODR platform was intended to offer consumers and traders a simple,
multilingual entry point for resolving cross-border disputes online, while support to ADR
schemes aimed to expand their availability, improve quality standards, and ensure consistent
coverage across the EU. The causal pathway linked the availability and accessibility of these
mechanisms to higher resolution rates, greater consumer confidence in seeking redress, and
ultimately improved market trust.
Objective IV: Support for ECC-Net and CPC sweeps → improved enforcement and consumer
support → higher trust in cross-border commerce.
Objective IV focused on enforcement, supporting joint actions between national authorities,
coordination through the CPC network, and the work of the ECCs. The Programme assumed
that better cooperation tools and training would lead to faster, more consistent enforcement of
consumer law across borders. Within this logic, CPC cooperation mechanisms, shared IT tools,
and targeted training were intended to strengthen cross-border case handling, facilitate timely
information exchange, and enable coordinated market surveillance actions. Support to ECCs
was designed to enhance assistance to consumers in cross-border cases, feeding intelligence
back into enforcement networks. The causal pathway linked these measures to intermediate
outcomes such as more efficient resolution of enforcement requests, greater consistency of
enforcement actions across Member States, and ultimately higher levels of consumer protection
in the internal market.
The evaluation tested these assumptions and causal links using a mix of quantitative and
qualitative methods. Indicators from Annex II of the Regulation were used to assess outputs,
including the number of RAPEX alerts, ECC contacts, ODR complaints, and grants awarded.
To evaluate outcomes and impacts, the assessment relied on the Consumer Scoreboard, ECC
and CPC network data, and key studies such as the 2017 research on measuring consumer
detriment. Focus groups, interviews, and project reporting also provided insights into
behavioural effects and enforcement practices, helping to validate or challenge the assumptions
embedded in the logic model.
Beyond its internal logic, the Programme’s outcomes were shaped by external factors. The
COVID-19 pandemic increased consumer vulnerability and accelerated digitalisation,
highlighting the need for flexible, digital-first tools while disrupting some enforcement
activities. Rapid growth in e-commerce introduced new challenges not foreseen at design stage.
Regional disparities in consumer awareness and institutional capacity also influenced
implementation success. Additionally, interaction with other EU initiatives (e.g. LIFE, Rights
4
and Equality, Consumer Agenda) created both synergies and attribution challenges. To assess
the effectiveness and coherence of the Programme, the intervention logic was not only
reconstructed but also used systematically throughout the evaluation as an analytical
framework.

External developments such as digitalisation, cross-border e-commerce, and COVID-19

HOW HAS THE SITUATION EVOLVED OVER THE EVALUATION PERIOD?
3.1 Programme management
The Programme was managed by DG Justice and Consumers and implemented by the
Consumer, Health, Agriculture and Food Executive Agency (CHAFEA) until its closure in
2021, after which responsibilities were transferred to the European Innovation Council and
SMEs Executive Agency (EISMEA). The transition affected the accessibility of data storage,
and documentation, creating challenges for the evaluation.
3.2 Programme implementation
The Commission implemented the Programme via annual work programmes. Funding was
provided through operating grants, action grants (including joint actions between Member
States), event grants, enforcement grants, and procurement contracts for studies, IT tools,
training, and awareness campaigns. Co-financing rates ranged from 50% to 95% (Article 8 of

calls for proposals, tenders, reimbursements, and indemnities.
3.3 Budget overview
The Programme was allocated a budget of EUR 188.8 million, with an additional EUR 5.6
million from EFTA countries (Norway and Iceland), bringing the total to EUR 194.4 million.
Of this, EUR 175.5 million was for operational commitments and EUR 18.9 million for
administrative and support costs, 64% of which went to executive agencies. Annual
commitments were stable, with a notable increase in 2019. Payments lagged behind
commitments, with no disbursement in 2014. From 2015 to 2024, EUR 169.9 million was
spent, yielding an absorption rate of 87.4%, higher than comparable programmes like LIFE
(64.1%) and Rights, Equality and Citizenship (84.2%).
Grants amounted to EUR 62.2 million, supporting 270 projects across 30 countries and 130
beneficiaries. Most funding went to Objective IV (69%), followed by Objective II (21%),
Objective I (8%), and Objective III (2%). Only seven projects were cross-border. Funding was
concentrated in Belgium, Germany, and the Netherlands, which received 47% of total grant
funds. Grants typically covered half of project costs. Procurement totaled EUR 107.7 million,
financing 573 contracts with 116 entities. While many contracts were under EUR 100,000,
large projects like RAPEX/Safety Gate, CASP, the ODR platform, and consumer campaigns
absorbed nearly half the budget. Procurement levels were steady (EUR 11 million/year) except
in 2019, when funding nearly doubled due to a shift from grants to procurement in key areas.
The total cost of the Programme is estimated at EUR 230 million. This includes EUR 194.4
million from the EU budget, and an estimated EUR 41.5 million in co-financing provided by
grant beneficiaries. The actual co-financing rates varied between 50% and 95% depending on
the type of action and beneficiary. Therefore, a weighted average co-financing rate of 60% was
applied to estimate the overall contribution from stakeholders. By objective, Objective II and
IV received the largest shares of funding (32% and 35%, respectively). Under Objective II,
Action 4 (evidence base) and Action 5 (support to consumer organisations) received the most
funding, while Action 7 (consumer education) saw notable growth. Under Objective I, Action
2 (market surveillance coordination) accounted for 86% of funding, with a 58% increase
between 2018–2019 following a strategic shift to procurement. Table 3 and Annex V provide
further detail on funded projects by year and activity.

EVALUATION FINDINGS (ANALYTICAL PART)
To what extent was the Consumer Programme successful and why?
4.1 Effectiveness
This section assesses whether activities funded delivered the expected outputs and contributed
to outcomes and impacts in line with the intervention logic. The evaluation found that the
Programme has been broadly effective in achieving its objectives.
Objective I: Product Safety
Objective I aimed to ensure a high level of product safety across the EU through activities
funded under Actions 1 to 3: provision of scientific advice, coordination of market surveillance
and enforcement, and risk analysis. Over 80% of the objective’s operational budget was
allocated to Action 2, especially via the Safety Gate/RAPEX system and CASP (Coordinated
Activities on Safety of Products).
The mid-term evaluation found that the funded activities were largely effective. Safety
Gate/RAPEX became a central pillar of EU market surveillance, enabling rapid cross-border
communication and information sharing between national authorities. Between 2014 and 2020,
over 14 000 alerts and 30 000 follow-up actions were recorded, demonstrating its expanding
reach18. However, achievement levels were influenced by limited staffing and financial
resources in national market surveillance authorities. Stakeholders noted the continued

complexity of items like connected devices and wearables. These trends demanded more agile
enforcement, straining existing capacities. Nonetheless, the Programme demonstrated strong
effectiveness through sustained investment in CASP and ongoing development of Safety
Gate/RAPEX, including new business reporting tools and better integration with national IT
systems19. The Safety Gate/RAPEX enables the rapid exchange of information between
national authorities on measures taken against products, thus facilitating coordinated actions
across the single market. It also provides accessible information to the wider public via its

Table 2 above presents progress under Objective I, based on two key indicators from the

with limited traceability, but by 2020 the rate climbed to 72%, far exceeding the 47.5% target
set. The reactions-per-notification ratio also improved from 1.28 in 2014 to 2.69 in 2020,
showing stronger cross-border cooperation. Safety Gate/RAPEX demonstrated its
effectiveness and agility, especially during the pandemic, for example, 25 million unsafe masks
were flagged in June 2020. In 2019–2020, alerts covered about 41.8 million products,
averaging 77,900 per notification, with 97% classified as serious risks22. Most notifications
concern serious risk (97%), highlighting the system’s focus on preventing the most dangerous
threats to consumer health and safety. Data quality also improved over the Programme period,
with fewer notifications missing key manufacturer details like batch numbers or barcodes.
However, gaps remain regarding product identification (e.g. model type), pointing to a need
for further improvements23. The steady volume of dangerous goods reported and followed up
through Safety Gate/RAPEX indicates that coordinated action and rapid communication have
helped reduce unsafe products in the EU market.
Focus group participants confirmed Safety Gate/RAPEX’s critical role in consumer protection
but identified areas for improvement. A key gap is the lack of linked accident or injury data,
which limits the ability to fully assess consumer safety impacts. Participants also stressed the
need for more harmonised risk assessments and regular training for national authorities.
Ongoing efforts, mainly through CASP, are addressing these challenges. Limited product
traceability, especially in complex global supply chains, remains a barrier to effective
enforcement. Participants suggested that allowing trusted external bodies (e.g. consumer
organisations) to submit structured alerts could enhance responsiveness. Some also noted that
they rarely receive follow-up from authorities after submitting product concerns, which
undermines feedback loops and system trust. Improved interoperability between Safety
Gate/RAPEX and ICSMS allowed faster data sharing and reduced duplication; by 2020, over
90% of national authorities used ICSMS to upload surveillance findings.

The mid-term evaluation found that, by the end of 2017, the Programme delivered mixed
results. It was effective in developing the evidence base, with Scoreboards and market studies
influencing consumer policy at both EU and national levels. It also successfully supported EU-
level consumer organisations, notably BEUC. However, consumer information and education
measures, such as the Consumer Champion training and Consumer Classroom, were less
effective. Although awareness campaigns met engagement targets, they had limited long-term
impact on consumer awareness. Key challenges included limited resources, lack of curriculum
integration, and the inability of training alone to overcome organisational capacity gaps. The
evaluation concluded that information campaigns had mixed results in contributing to the
Programme’s objectives. Despite earlier challenges, more recent campaigns showed improved
reach and engagement. Fully funded by the Programme, these educational efforts aimed to
boost awareness and confidence, particularly in cross-border online shopping. According to
interviews and literature, they helped inform consumers about their rights. The #YourEUright
campaign, targeting 18–35-year-olds, used social media, influencers, and interactive events
(e.g. escape rooms), reaching over 319 million contacts and generating 94 million
interactions38. Other specific campaigns included an information campaign to raise consumer
awareness on their rights39, a campaign targeting young consumers between 18 and 35 years

and promotion campaign for energy efficiency in households’ was conducted to guide decision-

campaign’s objectives were relevant, given low financial literacy levels in Austria and Czechia,

impact, raised only low awareness. Focus group and survey results showed no significant
increase in knowledge. Media coverage was modest, mostly found in financial sections

Objective III: Consumer rights and redress
Objective III aimed to support evidence-based consumer policy and improve access to redress.

Stakeholders in the mid-term evaluation confirmed these studies were effective and
recommended more targeted, smaller-scale research, a practice now adopted in the 2021–2027
SMP. According to focus groups, the studies directly shaped EU and national policymaking,
and supported legislation and enforcement. They also influenced how consumer vulnerability
is understood, reinforcing the concept of bounded rationality, and moving away from the
assumption of fully rational consumer behaviour.
Despite substantial efforts, the Programme did not significantly improve consumer access to
simple, low-cost redress mechanisms, particularly ADR. The ODR platform, launched in 2016
and fully funded by the Programme, aimed to provide a single EU entry point for online
consumer disputes. While communication efforts were highly effective, actual use remained
limited. Backed by a 2015 ex-ante evaluation, the ODR campaign exceeded expectations: it
reached 21 million users on Facebook, 9 million on Twitter, and generated 13 million video
views, four times the forecast. The platform saw 2.8 million visits in 2019, with 200,000
monthly users, and a Christmas campaign achieved 6.2 times more clicks than expected.
Activities also included branding, communications support, and outreach to traders, but these
efforts did not translate into widespread platform use.
Despite high visibility and traffic, the ODR platform saw very low conversion rates. Between
2016 to 2021, only about 1% of submitted complaints, fewer than 200 annually, were resolved
20
via ADR48. This remained unchanged despite technical upgrades and improved guidance. In
response, the Commission proposed repealing the ODR Regulation in October 2023, with the
repeal adopted in December 2024 and set to take effect in July 2025, citing the platform’s
persistent underperformance and limited added value.
Barriers to effectiveness extended beyond the ODR platform. While the Programme funded its
launch and extensive awareness campaigns, its overall impact on access to redress was limited
by the fragmented transposition of the ADR Directive across Member States. Compliance with
ODR obligations varied significantly by country, sector, and trader size, with larger traders and
some Member States engaging more, while smaller traders often lacked awareness or
willingness to participate. Inconsistent implementation, complex cross-border procedures, and
limited monitoring further weakened ADR reliability. Despite improvements to the platform’s
interface and communications, these systemic issues remained unresolved during the
Programme period.
Some stakeholder responses to the Call for Evidence expressed critical views on enforcement
and redress mechanisms under Objective IV. Organisations such as Next Energy Consumer
(NEC), DECO (Portugal), ITM (Poland), MSPCA (Malta), and individual citizens (e.g. from
Germany) raised concerns about limited access to justice and ineffective ADR mechanisms,
especially for vulnerable consumers. NEC cited structural barriers such as low trader
participation and lack of trust in redress tools. DECO and ITM noted slow and inconsistent
enforcement, while MSPCA highlighted a lack of responsive authorities in cross-border cases.
These concerns indicate that while the Programme provided tools like CPCS and ECC-Net,
some stakeholders found practical redress outcomes lacking, particularly in high-risk sectors
or for underrepresented consumers. They underline the need to clarify the Programme’s role
versus Member State responsibilities and highlight persistent gaps not reflected in indicator
data. Funding for ADR activities also underperformed. While 50 ADR grants were awarded
between 2018 and 2020, the budget was not fully absorbed. Key barriers included the 50% co-
financing requirement and administrative burden, especially for smaller ADR bodies.
Simplification efforts had limited effect. However, from 2022, the successor funding
programme, the SMP increased the EU co-financing to 90% and streamlined applications,
leading to a notable increase in uptake. ECCs also contributed to the Objective III by informing
consumers about ADR options and ODR platform. They did so through awareness-raising
campaigns on their national websites and social media channels, or physical stands in major
European cities e.g. around Black Friday, Christmas period or summer sales, etc. Many ADR
entities were awarded grants to raise awareness on out-of-court dispute resolution e.g.
conferences, TV and radio slots, etc.
The analysis of Objective III indicators shows mixed performance in facilitating consumer
redress. Of the three core indicators, only Indicator 1 (number of ODR complaints) met its
target, with 147,000 submissions by 2020, showing high initial uptake. However, Indicator 2
(proportion of unresolved ECC cases referred to ADR) reached just 24%, well below the 75%
target, and Indicator 3 (proportion of consumers acting on a problem) remained at 67%, missing
the 90% target (see Table 7). The broad definition of “complaint” in Indicator 3 (e.g. contacting
the seller, not just formal redress) limits its relevance for assessing ADR/ODR effectiveness.

disputes. Taken together, Scoreboard results confirm that the Programme helped build

by structural issues such as complexity, delays, and low trader accountability.

Objective IV: Enforcement
According to the mid-term evaluation, the Programme was successfully achieving Objective
IV by enhancing cooperation among national enforcement bodies and improving access to
enforcement-related advice for consumers. The CPC Network significantly expanded its
activities, becoming a cornerstone of EU consumer law enforcement. Mechanisms such as
mutual assistance, information exchange, and coordinated sweeps became more effective,
although handling times remained lengthy in some cases. CPC enforcement sweeps between
2014 and 2020 addressed sectors such as e-commerce, travel services, online reviews, and
misleading green claims, with non-compliance rates ranging from 42% to 78.7%. Most traders
corrected identified issues voluntarily, with enforcement action required in fewer than 18% of
cases. These actions contributed to notable improvements in compliance in targeted sectors.
Consumer trust in authorities and retailers increased, while reported consumer problems
slightly declined.
However, challenges remained. Stakeholders highlighted limited staffing and financial
resources in national authorities and the increasing complexity of products, services, and online
marketplaces as key obstacles. The CPC Network provided EU-wide added value by promoting
harmonised enforcement, supporting less-resourced authorities, and enabling best practice
exchange. Stakeholder support was strong: 15 of 19 responding national enforcement
24
authorities rated joint actions as “effective”, and sweeps were similarly well-regarded. Survey
and interview feedback confirmed the CPC’s relevance and the value of coordinated EU-level
enforcement. Capacity-building efforts were also central. Tools like the CPC Knowledge
Exchange Platform (CPC Wiki) and CPC Market Watch enhanced cooperation and risk
monitoring. The E-Enforcement Academy, launched in 2016, trained enforcement officials on
digital investigation skills through a mix of online and scenario-based modules. Performance
monitoring via the Single Market Scoreboard showed positive results: 66% of enforcement
requests were handled within 12 months (exceeding the 60% target), and 79% of information
requests were processed within three months (vs. a 50% target). These results demonstrate
improved efficiency and responsiveness across the CPC Network.
Enforcement cooperation and capacity building under Objective IV were core components
of the Programme’s effectiveness. From 2014 to 2020, a total of 859 exchanges of enforcement
officials took place, promoting standardised enforcement practices and cross-border
knowledge sharing. Survey responses from 7 participating national authorities rated the
exchange programme as effective (4) or very effective (2), with one neutral. While participation
varied by country, feedback confirmed its value.
Training for enforcement officials and the judiciary also received moderate to high
effectiveness ratings, reinforcing the importance of capacity-building. Other networking
activities, such as Presidency events and policy conferences, supported coordination efforts:
23 out of 24 respondents rated them as effective or very effective. The CPC Regulation (in
force since 2020) further strengthened enforcement coordination mechanisms. According to
the mid-term evaluation, two-thirds of retailers believed that public authorities actively monitor
compliance with consumer legislation, an observation confirmed by national and EU-level
interviews and stakeholder feedback. Sweeps were widely seen as effective by CPC
stakeholders, although some noted uneven implementation across countries. Capacity-building
tools, such as peer exchanges, training modules, CPC Wiki, and IT systems, were credited with
reinforcing enforcement capabilities and enabling cross-border cooperation.
Interviews with enforcement stakeholders (including CPC authorities, CSN, ECCs, BEUC,
ADR bodies, and Eurochambres) highlighted significant progress in capacity building, joint
enforcement, and knowledge sharing. However, gaps remain, especially in tackling complex,
evolving issues like greenwashing, where additional training and coordination are needed.
Survey respondents gave an average score of 4.2 ("Effective") for enforcement-related
activities. ECCs were rated closest to "Very Effective", and most respondents indicated that
intended benefits were “mostly achieved” in their country, showing strong alignment with the
Programme’s objectives.

within the CPC Network (see Table 2). The number of information exchange requests dropped
from 132 (2014) to 25 (2020), despite a brief rebound in 2018. Enforcement measure requests
peaked at 198 (2017) but fell to 113 (2020), indicating limited net progress. Alerts shared
within the CPC network consistently remained below the annual target of 82. Timeliness
indicators also underperformed: enforcement requests handled within 12 months fell short of
the 60% target and were later removed under the revised CPC Regulation (EU) 2017/2394.
Similarly, information requests handled within 3 months never reached the 50% target, ranging
between 23% and 38%. While the Programme supported training, coordination, and CPC

operations, it did not fund operational enforcement, limiting its direct influence on these results.
The worsening of some indicators reflects structural challenges across Member States,
particularly limited staffing, uneven prioritisation, and legal fragmentation.
In terms of wider impacts, consumer trust in public authorities rose slightly from 60% to 64%

declined, with only 66% in 2018 believing authorities monitor compliance, down from 75%

CPC coordination, and improved data monitoring under the new regulatory framework.

The evaluation assessed the costs of financing various activities under the Programme and
attempted to compare these with monetised benefits where such data was available. The

Objective I: Product safety
Safety Gate/RAPEX notifications, which alert national authorities and the public about
dangerous non-food products found on the EU market, have proven to be cost-effective. This
is because of these notifications’ impact on the number of accidents and ill-health consequences
avoided thanks to Member States follow-up actions upon receiving the notification. While it is
not possible to estimate the overall avoided detriment for consumers due to the lack of detailed
data on number and severity of avoided accidents, benefits would likely outweigh the costs of
Safety Gate/ RAPEX. This conclusion is further supported by the broader estimate from
product-related accidents, which amounts to approximately EUR 76.6 billion per year. Of this,
about 15%, equivalent to EUR 11.49 billion annually, is deemed preventable through improved

potential of preventive systems like Safety Gate/RAPEX in reducing avoidable harm.

A cost-benefit analysis of the ECCs confirmed a high level of efficiency and proportionality
under the Programme. ECCs were predominantly funded by grants, with EU co-financing
averaging 55, with those MS of low GDP receiving 67%. Annual EU funding rose from EUR
5.2 million in 2015 to EUR 7 million in 2020, supporting 29 ECCs, including centres in Iceland,
Norway, and the UK (until its withdrawal in 2020). France and Germany received the highest
total allocations (EUR 7.7 million each), due in part to their leadership of joint projects. Iceland
received the lowest funding (EUR 29 977–38 845). While most countries received a similar

the average cost per case declined from EUR 70 in 2014 to EUR 40 in 2020, demonstrating

the UK ECC had a high caseload but was not among the top five funded centres, likely due to

attracted additional co-financing. To assess proportionality, the evaluation estimated the
monetised value of ECC services. Using findings from the Commission’s consumer detriment
study, which identified financial loss, time lost, and psychological stress as key factors, a
simplified estimation was developed. Although ECC data do not perfectly match these
categories, the number of complaints handled between 2014 and 2020 allowed for a reasonable
approximation.

During this period, ECCs dealt with 130 781 complaints59. Applying an average financial

shared tools and practices. In particular, joint projects helped generate efficiency gains by
reducing duplication and allowing ECCs to leverage common infrastructure and
methodologies. Overall, ECCs are considered a success story within the Programme, delivering
both tangible consumer benefits and broader systemic value that support the case for continued
EU-level investment.
4.3 Coherence
The Programme was designed to be internally coherent across its four specific objectives.
Activities funded under each objective were intended to support complementary tools, data
flows, or actions, thereby reinforcing the broader goals of consumer protection, enforcement,
and information. Internal coherence was evident in several cross-cutting initiatives—for
example, how behavioural studies under Objective III were informed by research funded under
Objective II, or how data collected by ECCs (Objective IV) supported enforcement actions
under the CPC Network. Training tools such as the e-Enforcement Academy were designed to
serve multiple objectives, including product safety, market surveillance, and redress. Overall,
the evidence confirms the mid-term evaluation’s conclusion: the Programme was both
internally and externally coherent. While isolated areas showed room for improvement,
particularly in better linking networks like ECCs and the CPC, there were no significant
contradictions or overlaps identified. The Programme’s priorities and funded actions were
viewed as complementary and synergistic.

Objective IV: Enforcement
Activities funded under Objective IV, particularly the CPC Network and ECC Net, were found
mutually reinforcing and contributed to a coherent enforcement system that addressed both
collective consumer interests and individual assistance needs. While the CPC Network pursued
systemic infringements of EU consumer law, ECCs provided direct, cross-border support to
consumers. Their collaboration helped bridge the gap between policy enforcement and day-to-
day consumer redress. Cooperation between the ECC-Net and the CPC Network included joint
actions, such as coordinated response during the Covid-19 pandemic, when rogue traders
marketed fraudulent health products. Similar collaborations were reported in areas subscription
traps and other unfair commercial practices, where consumer complaints gathered by ECCs
informed CPC sweeps and investigations, linking Objective IV and III effectively. Synergies
also existed with BEUC, particularly in organising regular meetings and aligning advocacy on
enforcement gaps or systemic issues. Coherence in training and capacity building was
supported through initiatives such as the e-Enforcement Academy, which was also relevant to
Objective I, especially regarding product safety enforcement. The Academy provided market
surveillance and consumer enforcement authorities with access to harmonised training
materials, tools, and practices that strengthened cooperation and consistency across borders.
Despite these achievements, several stakeholders, particularly from ECCs, indicated that
synergies with the CPC Network could be further strengthened. Suggestions included
increasing the number and scope of joint activities, such as joint monitoring of emerging
commercial practices or coordinated responses to pan-European scams. The flow of
information between ECCs and ADR bodies was also seen as suboptimal, with feedback loops
often described as one-directional. During focus groups, ECC representatives noted that while
they regularly share intelligence with CPC and ADR bodies, they rarely receive systematic
updates or coordinated follow-up, limiting the potential to close the policy-practice loop.
Overall, Objective IV demonstrated solid internal coherence and contributed to enhancing the
overall enforcement ecosystem, yet further integration and feedback mechanisms between
networks and actors could significantly improve its impact.
External coherence
External coherence assesses the complementarity and alignment of the Programme with
broader EU consumer policy objectives and other relevant Union initiatives. Throughout the
2014-2020 period, the objectives and eligible actions of the Programme were coherent with
Article 169 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and with Article 38 of the
Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union which enshrines the right to a high level
of consumer protection, reinforcing the Programme’s role in safeguarding consumer rights and
promoting fair market practices across the EU. It supported the practical implementation of the
vision outlined in the Consumer Agenda 2012 and Digital Single Market Strategy 2015. There
was also a significant degree of coherence between the objectives of the Programme and the
2018 New Deal for Consumers. Since the last set of commitments under the Programme were

made in 2020 and their implementation thus goes beyond 2020, the evaluation assessed
coherence with the 2020 Consumer Agenda66 that builds on the 2012 agenda and addresses
new and emerging challenges, including the Covid-19 pandemic, digital transformation and
green transition.
The Programme contributed to the EU's strategy for smart, sustainable, and inclusive growth
by improving consumer confidence, market transparency, and regulatory coherence—all
essential enablers of competitiveness. By reinforcing trust in digital and cross-border
transactions, supporting informed decision-making, and enabling dispute resolution, the
Programme reduced friction in internal market functioning and stimulated both consumer and
business activity.
Several Programme elements were directly conducive to smart, sustainable and inclusive
growth by strengthening the position of consumers as informed, empowered and protected
actors in the internal market: 1. Actions supporting digital transition (e.g. consumer education
on digital rights, ODR, BEUC’s work on platform regulation) improved digital market
confidence. 2. CASP and RAPEX helped create safer product markets, thereby fostering a fair
competitive environment. 3. ADR and ECC-Net contributed to business competitiveness by
reducing costly litigation and improving customer satisfaction. 4. Capacity-building for SMEs
through Consumer Law Ready reduced compliance burdens and increased trust in SME offers.
Less growth-relevant areas included awareness campaigns with limited long-term behavioural
effects and the underperforming ODR platform, which had lower practical uptake by
consumers and traders.
Overall, the aims and objectives of the Programme complemented those of the other EU
funding programmes, contributing to a comprehensive approach to consumer protection,
environmental sustainability, social equality, and market integration within the EU. This also
suggests that the activities funded under the Programme were coherent with broader EU
policies. In relation to broader EU policies, Article 12 of the TFEU commits the EU to taking
consumer protection requirements into account in ‘defining and implementing other Union
policies and activities’. A significant degree of coherence between the Programme and the
following programmes has been identified:
• With the LIFE Programme, coherence was found in environmental goals, particularly
in promoting sustainable consumption practices and eco-labelling, though LIFE’s focus
is broader and more environmentally anchored.
• With the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF), coherence emerged particularly in the
digital domain, where CEF funded digital infrastructure while the Programme
supported digital consumer empowerment, such as through ODR and consumer
education on digital rights.
• With the Rights, Equality and Citizenship (REC) Programme, coherence was
ensured through internal coordination within DG JUST, avoiding duplication despite
thematic overlap. While REC covered broader social issues, it included a specific
objective on consumer rights. Funded actions, averaging EUR 1.3 million annually,
were small-scale and complementary, focusing on digital consumer protection, capacity

Objective I: Product safety
The external coherence of coordinated market surveillance and alerts was high, as these actions
supported enforcement of, and disseminated data relevant to, on a wide range of EU product
safety legislation, including GPSD and various sectoral directives. The Safety Gate/RAPEX
system served as a key instrument in sharing information on dangerous non-food products
across Member States and with external partners, thereby supporting consistent
implementation of EU law and enhancing market surveillance coordination. The exchanges of
enforcement officials, through joint actions and CASP projects, contributed to a more
harmonised and coherent approach to surveillance across the EU. International cooperation
reinforces the external coherence of the Programme by ensuring that EU actions in product
safety and market surveillance are aligned with broader international frameworks and partner
initiatives. The Commission’s active participation in global fora such as the OECD Global
Recall System and International Product Safety Week not only supports the exchange of best
practices, but also ensures complementarity with global efforts. Examples such as the
reciprocal data-sharing with Health Canada and the adoption of EU-led product safety pledges
by other jurisdictions underscore the Programme’s alignment with international norms and its
contribution to globally coherent consumer protection frameworks. These efforts help avoid
duplication, enhance trust, and ensure consistent standards in an increasingly interconnected
global marketplace.
Objective II: Consumer information and education, developing the evidence base and
support to consumer organisations
The support provided to BEUC, as the main grant beneficiary under Objective II, significantly
enhanced the external coherence of the Consumer Programme. BEUC acted as a key interface
between EU consumer policy and both internal and external policymaking arenas. At the EU
level, it ensured alignment between consumer protection priorities and broader strategies such
as the Digital Single Market, the Green Deal, and the Capital Markets Union by actively
contributing to legislative processes and coordinating the input of its national members.
Externally, BEUC represented EU consumer interests in global fora including the OECD,
ICPEN, and the Trans-Atlantic Consumer Dialogue, ensuring consistency between the
Programme’s objectives and evolving international consumer policy standards. Its cooperation
with ANEC and regular interaction with ECCs and CPC authorities further reinforced policy
alignment across standardisation, enforcement, and redress mechanisms. Other activities under
Objective II also demonstrated a high degree of external coherence. Programmes such as

Objective IV: Enforcement
The funding provided under Objective IV was externally coherent with the overall EU legal

sector-specific actors, such as civil aviation authorities on passenger rights, travel and hotel
agents, trade unions, and major e-commerce platforms. These efforts complemented the work
of national consumer organisations, reinforcing the EU’s consumer protection architecture.

4.4 How did the EU intervention make a difference and to whom?
The mid-term evaluation of the Programme highlighted that funded activities, such as Safety
Gate/RAPEX, the CPC Network, ECC-Net and support to BEUC, have generated clear EU
added value. This was particularly evident where actions complemented national measures by
addressing cross-border challenges, enabling economies of scale, or creating synergies that
could not have been achieved by Member States acting alone. The Programme facilitated more
effective collaboration among national authorities, enabled the sharing of best practices, and
allowed resources to be pooled to achieve common goals, contributions widely recognised as
valuable by stakeholders responding to the survey and other consultations.
The EU intervention through the Programme made a tangible difference to European
consumers, especially in cross-border contexts where national measures alone would have been
insufficient. It provided tools, networks, and enforcement mechanisms that ensured consumers
could shop more safely, resolve disputes more easily, and access reliable information,
regardless of where they lived. Activities such as Safety Gate/RAPEX, ECC-Net, CASP, and
the CPC Network helped to harmonise protection levels across the Single Market, supporting
trust in product safety, e-commerce, and redress. Quantitative and qualitative evidence
confirms that consumers were the primary beneficiaries. For instance, the ECC-Net is
estimated to have generated at least EUR 23.4 million in direct consumer benefits through
complaints handled and guidance offered. Nevertheless, quantifying the difference or impact
of the Programme on consumers remains challenging, quantifying the difference or impact of
the Programme on consumers is challenging, as the Programme was not designed with a strong
counterfactual evaluation framework, and many of its broader effects were not directly tracked.
Equally, the Programme’s impact on competitiveness and economic growth was primarily
indirect and not always quantifiable. While it likely contributed to a fairer business
environment and more efficient markets, especially in cross-border trade, the evaluation
acknowledges the difficulty in attributing specific macroeconomic outcomes (e.g. increased
GDP or innovation) directly to Programme actions.
Stakeholders consistently emphasised that EU support was essential to ensuring consistent
services across the Single Market and building consumer confidence, particularly in areas such
as product safety, cross-border trade, the digital economy, and e-commerce. Specific
achievements, such as the promotion of ADR mechanisms in sectors like telecommunications
and postal services, were viewed as directly dependent on EU-level intervention. EU funding
was also seen as critical for enabling capacity-building, training, policy development and
enforcement actions. Many stakeholders noted that, without sustained EU support, national
public resources would likely have been insufficient to achieve similar outcomes, potentially
resulting in fragmentation and weakened consumer protection, especially in Member States
with more limited capacity. However, some stakeholders expressed more critical or nuanced
views. These included concerns about uneven access to consumer protection tools across
Member States, the limited practical reach of certain actions, particularly in redress and
enforcement, and the underperformance of specific initiatives, such as the ODR platform. Civil
society and consumer organisations also pointed to areas where enforcement could be
strengthened, and consumer education further enhanced. These perspectives underline the
40
importance of ensuring that future actions are both inclusive and adaptable to national contexts,
and that they respond to gaps in impact, especially in domains with weaker infrastructures.
Compliant businesses also benefitted through improved legal clarity, a more level playing field,
and increased consumer trust in cross-border transactions.
Objective I: Product safety
Sharing and streamlining information on unsafe consumer products through Safety
Gate/RAPEX identified by a Member State with other Member States avoided duplication in
the identification and investigation of unsafe products and enabled a co-ordinated approach to
market surveillance and enforcement. This system, coupled with harmonised market
surveillance, ensured that products met the same safety standards regardless of where they were
sold, reinforcing the integrity of the Single Market. By pooling resources and expertise, by
sharing risk assessment practices and building trust between authorities, CASP projects
reduced the administrative burden of testing, allowing for comprehensive testing and efficient
market surveillance while avoiding duplication of efforts - achievements that would be difficult
for Member States to attain individually. CASP also facilitated development of methodologies
and ways of working that are based on good practices from around the EU through its horizontal
activities.
Objective II: Consumer information and education, developing the evidence base and
support to consumer organisations
EU-funded awareness initiatives, such as campaigns on online shopping and travel or e-
learning platforms, delivered stronger results than national efforts alone by ensuring a
harmonised approach and avoiding disparities in information quality across Member States.
Centralised coordination also enabled more efficient use of resources. Interviewees, including
representative from national consumer organisations, BEUC, and DG JUST officials noted that
these initiatives improved consumer access to reliable information and support. BEUC’s cross-
border activities added clear EU value by supporting national consumer organisations,
coordinating collective redress, and contributing to high-profile cases such as Dieselgate and
the Google Shopping antitrust appeal. Its policy input helped shape key initiatives like the New
Deal for Consumers and informed EU rules on digital markets, financial services, and green
claims. BEUC also supported enforcement by helping national organisations act on large-scale
consumer harm and by contributing expertise to international forums. This strengthened the
capacity of national organisations, particularly in smaller Member States, and ensured more
consistent consumer protection across the EU.
Within Consumer PRO and Consumer Law Ready the national level activities benefited
from European level support and coordination, ensuring a consistent level of service across
MS, while maintaining topics and training tailored to the MS. The Consumer PRO European
workshops were well-received, with feedback noting that companies are international, and can
use their resources more effectively by learning from other countries70. While EU interventions
in the field of consumer education and information contributed to some improvement, it cannot
be argued that the changes resulted directly from EU interventions, rather than other factors.
Arguably, the impact of EU interventions is higher in the Member States with lower budgets

Objective III: Consumer rights and redress
Analysis of evidence related to Objective III confirms the added value of EU interventions.
Persistent disparities in the results of the Consumer Conditions Scoreboard71 highlight the
ongoing need for EU-level action. Behavioural studies contributed to this by sharing findings
with Member States that lacked the capacity to conduct such research themselves, thereby
supporting evidence-based policy and regulatory improvements. Additional EU added value
came through the commissioning of consumer market analyses, legal gap assessments, and
application reports, which informed policy development. A citation analysis showed that
behavioural studies were frequently referenced in documents supporting legislation and that
some recommendations were incorporated into EU initiatives. While direct evidence of
behavioural studies influencing enforcement or voluntary practices remains limited, there are
indications that some enforcement actions, such as sweeps in the areas of consumer credit and
online travel websites, have followed themes identified in behavioural studies. Similarly, the
updated Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) guidance72 includes enforcement
examples relevant to online platforms and social media.
The Programme supported the implementation of the ODR Regulation and the ODR platform,
by providing the necessary infrastructure and accompanying measures to promote their use.
While the ODR platform established a unified, centralised channel for dispute resolution,
particularly useful for Member States with less developed systems, the low success rate of
resolved cases limited its overall EU added value73. The Programme also supported the
implementation of the ADR Directive by funding activities that promoted access to quality out-
of-court resolution for consumers across the EU, especially in cross-border contexts. Grants to
ADR entities typically ranged from EUR 10 000 to EUR 60 000, co-financing up to 50% of
eligible costs. These grants supported awareness-raising activities, case handling
improvements, staff training, and exchanges of best practices. In 2020, and again under the
2024 call for proposals, the Programme allocated dedicated budgets (e.g. €1 million in 2024)
to enhance the capacity of ADR entities and qualified consumer organisations. Interviewed
stakeholders, including representatives of ADR entities and national competent authorities,
highlighted that Programme-funded networking and training initiatives helped improve
consistency and visibility of ADR mechanisms across Member States. Given that nearly half
of complaints submitted via the ODR platform concerned cross-border cases, the Programme’s
support for ADR capacity and cooperation provided meaningful EU added value, particularly
in Member States where national systems remained underdeveloped.

Objective IV: Enforcement
Activities funded under Objective IV related to the CPC Network have provided significant
EU added value, which is widely acknowledged by stakeholders, including CPC authorities,
ECCs, consumer organisations, ADR entities, DG JUST officials in both mid-term evaluation

strengthening national measures, through joint actions, networking and training of enforcement
officials. In addition, the Commission’s coordination activities and support of enforcement
against international companies, ensured an improved level playing field across the Single
Market. Stakeholders explained that as e-commerce had been steadily growing and exploded
in 2020, it made the Commission’s coordination and tools like web crawlers even more
essential for CPC authorities to respond effectively. They also emphasised that without
financing and developing these tools, it would have been very difficult for Member States to
react to the rapid changes in e-commerce and technological advancements.
The ECC-Net played a crucial role in cross-border trade by assisting with disputes and
ensuring consistent service across all centres. Better-resourced ECCs supported those with
fewer resources, allowing for a uniform level of service regardless of location. This
collaboration ensured that consumers, wherever they were, received reliable assistance with
cross-border issues, demonstrating the added value of the EU's support. ECC-Net's contribution
to consumer confidence extended to the digital economy. By helping consumers trust the
internal market, the network enabled cross-border purchases of goods and services, benefiting
both consumers and businesses. This was validated by ECC representatives, who emphasized
the importance of the network in building trust in cross-border trade and supporting the Single
Market. Prior to joining ECC-Net, some centres74 only dealt with national complaints, but the
network's resources allowed them to expand their support to cross-border issues. Thanks to the
CPC Regulation, many ECCs were designated to send external alerts related to existing and
potential infringements which were made directly available to the CPC network; hence
contributing to a more robust EU enforcement toolbox.
4.5 Is the intervention still relevant?
The evidence from this evaluation confirms the ongoing relevance and appropriateness of the
Programme’s objectives. These objectives remain aligned with the needs of consumers across
the EU, especially in light of the continued digitalisation, globalisation, and emergence of new
market risks related to AI, sustainability, and cross-border digital commerce. Activities, such
as market surveillance, consumer education and cross-border dispute resolution, continue to
address systems risks and ensure fair treatment of consumers in an evolving internal market.
The increasing demand for cross-border dispute resolution and the need for stronger
cooperation among enforcement stakeholders highlights the continued relevance of the
Programme, particularly in light of emerging e-commerce and AI-related safety concerns. The
mid-term evaluation found the Programme addressed the needs and problems identified at the
Programme’s outset, with the exception of limited targeting of vulnerable consumers. The
Programme’s actions were able to adapt to the changing consumer needs, particularly as

4.6 Further evaluation criteria
Utility: The evidence supports the continued usefulness of the Programme’s objectives and
actions, across all four objectives. In particular, the Programme adapted to emerging challenges
faced by consumers in the context of digitalisation and globalisation. It successfully addressed
product safety concerns, benefiting vulnerable groups, including children. Tools such as Safety
Gate/RAPEX and CASPs strengthened market surveillance, contributed to improve the safety
of products placed on the market. While information sharing, awareness-raising campaigns,
and educational initiatives remained essential, they were often seen as less useful for consumer
groups due to how they were designed and implemented. Nevertheless, the growing demand
for cross-border dispute resolution and for enhanced cooperation among enforcement
authorities underlines the ongoing utility of the Programme, especially in the context of e-
commerce and AI-related safety concerns. These are increasingly being addressed 87revised
legislation￼ and initiatives funded under the Single Market Programme. The utility of the
cooperation networks was evident, for example, in the activities of the CPC and ECC networks.
Overall, the Programme was largely useful, with room for improvement in addressing
stakeholder concerns and better responding to consumer needs.

Union legislation for the coordination of enforcement actions between Member States. By
pooling resources through platforms like Rapid Alert System, the Programme ensured a
comprehensive approach to identifying and addressing dangerous products. Harmonisation
efforts, such as EU-wide follow-ups and coordinated activities, like joint sweeps aimed to
establish consistent consumer protection standards and enforcement practices.
Equity: was assessed by examining how equitably the Programme’s effects were distributed
across regions, stakeholders, and vulnerable consumers. The evaluation revealed disparities in
Member State participation, partly due to language barriers. Efforts to improve accessibility,
such as translating Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts into all EU languages (since 2018) and
simplifying user interfaces, helped mitigate this. Despite continued regional differences,
particularly in consumer conditions across eastern and southern EU countries, progress toward
narrowing the gap was observed. The Consumer Markets Scoreboard showed that financial
status influenced consumer experiences, with financially struggling individuals reporting lower
satisfaction and less likelihood to seek redress. BEUC addressed some vulnerability issues,
such as energy poverty, payment fraud, and vulnerable borrowers, but broader attention to
vulnerable groups was limited. Children were primarily mentioned in the context of unsafe
toys, and one cosmetics risk assessment lacked adequate consideration of vulnerable users.
Overall, Programme outputs addressing vulnerable consumers were limited and concentrated
in 2017–2020, mainly via behavioural studies. In a sample of 97 funded projects, only five
explicitly targeted vulnerable groups. These findings partially align with EESC concerns,
which called for earlier and more systematic integration of vulnerable consumer needs across
all Programme objectives88.
