Sustainability: The sustainability of the effects of interventions showed a mixed picture, but
on the whole most funded actions will have long lasting results. Regulatory measures supported
by the Programme have resulted in enduring structural changes. Ongoing alert services, such
as the Rapid Alert System, ensure continuous monitoring of product safety. Risk assessments
and scientific opinions remain relevant until updated due to new discoveries. Platforms like the
ODR platform provided a foundation for sustained consumer protection in online transactions.
Although a decision to discontinue the ODR platform has been made, useful elements of it such
as the database of ADR bodies will continue to be used. The impact of the Programme on
international systems was not well documented in the literature reviewed.
Acceptability was assessed based on how well the Programme’s interventions aligned with
consumer needs, higher alignment typically signals greater acceptability. The Programme
demonstrated strong alignment, as seen in BEUC’s advocacy during Dieselgate, enforcement
actions addressing penalty gaps, and the emphasis on product safety and authority cooperation.
Internally, actions were implemented with a high degree of coherence. The evaluation also
examined the Programme’s role in ensuring a consistent level of consumer protection across
the EU and EEA. Despite some coordination challenges for EU-level associations and varying
national collective redress procedures, mechanisms like Safety Gate/RAPEX and CPC joint
actions significantly contributed to harmonised enforcement and responses. To identify shifts
in perception, historical and current stakeholder and public views were compared. Public
perception was influenced by several factors, including high-profile product safety incidents
such as the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 overheating issue.
5.
WHAT ARE THE CONCLUSIONS AND LESSONS LEARNED?
5.1 Conclusions
The ex-post evaluation demonstrated that the Programme has been broadly effective with
regard to its main objective and the four specific objectives, efficient and had EU added value.
It was coherent and relevant. However, while the available indicators provide evidence of
outputs and immediate results, their fitness for tracking long-term impact remains limited.
Several indicators remained output-focused, and few were linked to baseline or target values,
making it difficult to measure changes in consumer detriment or business compliance. The
evaluation relied on triangulated qualitative data, interviews, focus groups, stakeholder
surveys, to fill these gaps, but acknowledged the limitations of these sources, particularly the
non-representative nature of the 57-survey responses and the likely selective memory bias.
Where observational data (e.g. Scoreboard trust metrics, market outcomes) were available, they
were used to reinforce the conclusions, but cannot be interpreted as directly attributable effects
due to the absence of a counterfactual.
Regarding effectiveness, the evaluation demonstrated that the Programme has been broadly
effective in achieving its objectives. Under Objective I, Safety Gate/RAPEX significantly
improved cross-border product safety coordination, reduced disparities in market surveillance,
and contributed to greater consumer confidence in cross-border shopping. The Coordinated
Activities on the Safety of Products (CASP) benefited national authorities, businesses, and
consumer organisations—particularly in recall effectiveness and informing legislation.
However, challenges remain due to unequal enforcement resources among Member States and
ongoing difficulties integrating scientific advice into regulatory processes. Maintaining
consistent standards and coordination across Member States continues to require attention.
48
Under Objective II, BEUC’s activities effectively coordinated national consumer
organisations and ensured their input into EU policymaking on digital, environmental, and
financial issues, including those affecting vulnerable consumers. In contrast, other consumer
awareness and education initiatives, despite achieving outreach metrics, had limited long-term
impact on consumer knowledge and trust, as reflected in Consumer Scoreboard data. Structural
challenges, including low integration into national curricula and declining NGO trust, hindered
broader effectiveness. Programmes like Consumer Law Ready and Consumer PRO performed
strongly, meeting targets and adapting well to online delivery during COVID-19, with reported
improvements in knowledge and behaviour. However, Consumer Champion and Consumer
Classroom underperformed due to low engagement, lack of localisation, and weak alignment
with national systems.
Under Objective III, the Programme was moderately effective in supporting consumer rights
and access to redress. Behavioural and market studies were a key strength, informing major
policy initiatives (e.g. Consumer Credit Directive, UCPD) and cited as good practice
internationally. However, their direct enforcement impact was limited. The ODR platform
reached visibility and usage targets, but its resolution rate remained extremely low (~1%),
mainly due to limited trader participation. While ADR structures benefited from grants and
training, uptake and awareness remained uneven across the EU, and key performance
indicators were not achieved. Progress was made in strengthening redress infrastructure, but
systemic and legal limitations undermined its full potential.
Under Objective IV, the Programme effectively supported cross-border enforcement through
the CPC Network and ECC-Net, though with mixed results. ECCs consistently exceeded
targets for consumer contacts and website visits, proving effective especially in countries with
fewer resources. Conversely, CPC Network performance indicators showed declining
effectiveness, notably in the timeliness and number of enforcement actions. Nonetheless,
stakeholder feedback strongly supported the added value of EU-level coordination, the CPCS
IT platform, and joint enforcement actions—particularly for tackling online infringements. The
Programme helped maintain a minimum level of enforcement capacity across Member States,
but uneven national commitment and resourcing continued to constrain outcomes.
With regards to efficiency, under Objective I, the Programme demonstrated high efficiency
by pooling resources and coordinating market surveillance activities. CASP projects were cost-
effective, enabling joint product testing at significantly lower average costs compared to
national testing. The integration of Safety Gate/RAPEX with ICSMS further enhanced
efficiency by improving information flows and avoiding duplication. However, efficiency
varied across Member States due to differences in administrative capacity and levels of national
funding.
Under Objective II, efficiency outcomes were mixed. Initiatives like Consumer Law Ready
and Consumer PRO achieved strong economies of scale and consistent training quality across
Member States, making effective use of EU coordination. In contrast, digital outreach tools
such as Consumer Champion and Consumer Classroom showed limited efficiency due to low
uptake and weak sustainability, despite considerable resource inputs. The BEUC operating
49
grant was generally considered efficient given its broad coordination role, but limited
availability of detailed cost and output data prevented a full assessment.
Under Objective III, efficiency was undermined by the low cost-effectiveness of the ODR
platform, which incurred substantial investment but resolved only a small number of disputes.
By contrast, ADR mechanisms—when used—proved more cost-efficient for consumers,
traders, and Member States. Grants supporting the digitalisation of ADR and the exchange of
best practices improved efficiency at the organisational level. However, the full potential of
these grants was not realised, as funding uptake was limited and the Programme was unable to
disburse its full allocations.
Under Objective IV, ECCs showed high efficiency by consistently meeting increasing
consumer demand without significant increases in EU funding. Their collaborative structure
enabled more resourced centres to assist others, boosting overall network performance. CPCS
activities were more variable: while joint enforcement actions and training helped reduce
fragmentation, several performance indicators declined or stagnated. This was partly due to
uneven national investment and administrative burdens. Stakeholders highlighted the
importance of Commission coordination, which was viewed as a necessary and efficient
enabler, though returns on investment varied by Member State.
On internal coherence, the Programme’s four objectives were broadly complementary and
mutually reinforcing. Actions funded under different objectives (e.g. behavioural studies under
Objective III informing campaigns under Objective II, or ADR capacity-building supporting
ECC work under Objective IV) demonstrated functional synergy. Internal coherence was
evident in the alignment between educational initiatives, enforcement coordination, and
consumer information. However, some gaps persisted, particularly in the underexploited
collaboration between ECCs and the CPC Network, and the limited integration of ECCs with
ADR entities in sharing practices and feedback mechanisms.
On external coherence, the Programme was well aligned with EU consumer law, notably
Article 169 TFEU and Article 38 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, which require a high
level of consumer protection. It supported implementation of the 2012 Consumer Agenda and
ensured coherence with EU strategies such as the Digital Single Market, the Green Deal, and
sustainability policy. Its tools and funding filled important implementation gaps in EU
consumer acquis, and complemented other EU programmes, such as the Rights, Equality and
Citizenship Programme and the LIFE Programme, without duplication.
With regards to EU added value, the Programme demonstrably enabled actions that Member
States or stakeholders could not have undertaken independently. This includes coordinated
enforcement actions through CPC and CASP, cross-border complaint handling via ECCs,
supranational behavioural research, and harmonised training platforms like Consumer Law
Ready. Interviewees and focus group participants confirmed that EU-level intervention was
essential for scale, consistency, and legitimacy, particularly in cross-border contexts, digital
markets, and areas where national capacity was weak.
On relevance, the Programme remained well aligned with consumer needs throughout the
2014–2020 period, adapting to key structural shifts such as digitalisation, the rise of online
50
platforms, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Its focus areas, product safety, redress, information,
and enforcement, addressed persistent and emerging risks. While the needs of vulnerable
consumers were not always sufficiently targeted, the Programme overall retained its policy
relevance, as confirmed by both stakeholder feedback and independent evidence (e.g.
Scoreboards, complaint data, Safety Gate/RAPEX alerts). The continued inclusion of the same
objectives in the SMP 2021–2027 reflects this enduring alignment.
5.2 Lessons learned
Throughout the evaluation several areas for improvement have been identified:
• Ensure consistent data collection and record keeping, so as to enable evaluations
of funding programmes: a consistent, systematic, comprehensive and accurate
method for recording documentation, including a list of all funded projects and a
comprehensive set of project data records required for evaluation shall be established.
Data consistency across all funded activities, including data on outputs, and results shall
be improved.
• Further develop indicators to better monitor impact: Develop outcome and impact
indicators that focus on the quality of deliverables and achieved results. Measurement
should expand beyond the simple numerical indicators and should also focus to capture
quality, e.g. the quality of BEUC’s interactions with policy makers in terms of influence
they have had, rather than just the number of meetings or presentations. For ECCs and
the CPC network, for example indicators should focus on the nature and extent of the
actions taken or results for consumers.
• Streamline campaigns, and information and education provision: Strengthen the
role of BEUC and national consumer organisations in information and education
activities to enhance the impact and reach of consumer protection initiatives across the
EU. Limit EU communication campaigns to key topics targeting consumer awareness.
Enhance consumer education through diversified communication channels and
strengthen school programmes to include consumer-related information.
• Maximise the use of behavioural studies to support policy-making and
enforcement: Continue conducting studies supporting policy-making and initiate
studies to support CPC authorities. Conduct both large and smaller studies to ensure
more flexibility and keep them supra-national to address common concerns across
Member States. Increase access to data supporting policy-making, particularly for
academic scholars and consumer organisations.
• Strengthen co-operation and communication between national actors to further
build capacity: Promote networking and collaboration and creating further synergies
by joint planning of and outreach about activities and encourage greater sharing of
knowledge, data and expertise, as well as tools and approaches. Revise how impacts of
joint working are captured. Continue with joint training initiatives to build capacities at
national level.
• Strengthen the Safety Gate/RAPEX: Continue ensuring that Safety Gate reflects the
new General Product Safety Regulation by, amongst others, enabling direct consumer
reporting of unsafe products through the Consumer Safety Gateway, facilitating closer
interaction between online marketplaces and national authorities through the Safety
Business Gateway, and improved interoperability between systems like the Information
and Communication System on Market Surveillance (ICSMS), Safety Gate, etc.

Continue providing opportunities for common risk assessments through CASP or other
formats, and keep the CASP framework agile and responsive to emerging risks and
unexpected situations such as COVID-19.
• Streamline support for and obligations to participate in ADRs: Further simplify the

improve handling times for enforcement requests within the CPC network. Expand and
upgrade IT tools to enhance coordination and response times across Member States.
Continue investing in e-enforcement training to equip authorities for the challenges of
digital marketplaces. Strengthen cross-border enforcement efforts through joint actions
and peer-to-peer meetings. Foster increased cooperation between the CPC Network and
ECC Net. Also in the area of product safety, make use of all enforcement options that
the GPSR provides for, including for example sweeps.
